dsh_event_bus.What problem does an event bus solve in: Plugins need to react to or change core behavior without the core knowing them. A bus decouples the parts that raise events from the plugins that handle them.
dsh_event_bus.Explain the difference between emit, bai: emit: call everyone, ignore results. bail: return the first value that is not None or False. serial and parallel: async, in order or concurrently. waterfall: middleware wrapping next(). An approval check fits bail or serial; a timeout wrapper fits waterfall.
dsh_event_bus.Why snapshot the listener list at the st: A listener may add or remove listeners while the dispatch is running. Without a snapshot, some are skipped, run twice, or the loop breaks.
dsh_event_bus.Walk through how next() in a waterfall f: Each listener gets a next() that calls the following listener or the inner function. Calling it twice runs the rest of the chain twice.
dsh_event_bus.Why should registration return a dispose: The disposer removes exactly that registration, even if the same function was registered twice. It also closes over the correct list.
dsh_event_bus.Should a failing emit listener stop the: Stopping lets one buggy plugin break everything, while containing the error keeps the others running but can hide the failure. Log it either way.
dsh_event_bus.Waterfall middleware versus explicit hoo: Waterfalls compose flexibly but ordering bugs are hard to see. Explicit hooks are easier to trace but need core changes for each new extension point.

dsh_tool_admission.How does an agent harness decide whether: Middleware decides allow, deny, ask (a human) or cancel (abort). Then ask is resolved and guards can still deny.
dsh_tool_admission.Why must a call that needs approval be d: With no approval channel there is nobody to say yes. Failing closed is the only safe default.
dsh_tool_admission.Walk through how next() chains the polic: next() calls the following middleware, and the last one returns allow. A middleware that does not call next() short-circuits: later ones never run.
dsh_tool_admission.Why do guards run after all middleware,: Middleware can override each other. Guards run last, only after an allow, and can only deny, so no plugin order can undo a guard.
dsh_tool_admission.After the user approves a call, should g: Yes: approval covers the user's intent, but a guard encodes hard limits (sandbox, budget) that no approval should bypass.
dsh_tool_admission.Approval per call versus per session ver: Per-call approval is safest but tiring, and per-session is convenient but a prompt injection can abuse it. Allow-lists are fast but need maintenance.
dsh_tool_admission.Policy as code (middleware) versus polic: Code can express anything but is hard to audit. Data rules are reviewable and diffable but limited.

dsh_tool_dispatch.Why must every tool call, including a de: Model APIs require one result per call id. A missing result invalidates the transcript and the model never learns what happened.
dsh_tool_dispatch.What is around-middleware on tool execut: Timeouts, retries, metrics and sandboxing: wrap the body without changing the tool.
dsh_tool_dispatch.Why are the body's exceptions caught ins: Then the around-middleware still receives a normal error result, and a middleware bug is not mistaken for a tool error.
dsh_tool_dispatch.Walk through accept versus block. Why do: Accept keeps or edits the result, while block replaces it with feedback. The tool's own contexts no longer apply to a result it did not produce.
dsh_tool_dispatch.Why do denied and cancelled calls still: Policies such as the repeat-call reminder must see every attempt, including refused ones, to detect loops.
dsh_tool_dispatch.Letting post-execute policies rewrite or: Rewriting is powerful (redaction, blocking) but hides what the tool really returned. Log the original to keep it auditable.
dsh_tool_dispatch.Returning tool errors to the model versu: Transient errors (network, rate limits) belong in harness retries. Errors about the arguments or the task should go back to the model.

dsh_tool_timeout.What is the difference between cooperati: Cooperative: the tool checks a signal and stops itself; preemptive: it is killed from outside. Killing can leave files or processes half-changed.
dsh_tool_timeout.What does combining an upstream cancel s: A tool stops when either the caller aborts or its timer fires. Reporting the first cause keeps the reason accurate.
dsh_tool_timeout.Walk through the timeout wrapper: why sw: The execution gets a combined signal for the duration. finally restores the caller's signal even when the tool raises.
dsh_tool_timeout.Deadlines nest: a turn deadline fires wh: Each deadline aborts with a TimeoutReason carrying its own code. The wrapper reports a tool timeout only when timeout_of(signal, "TOOL_TIMEOUT") matches, so when the turn deadline (another code) fires, the tool's own result passes through.
dsh_tool_timeout.Why must the wrapper keep waiting for th: The tool may still be writing. Returning early would let the next step run concurrently with a tool that has not finished.
dsh_tool_timeout.What do you do about a tool that ignores: Grace then kill is simple but can corrupt state, and process isolation makes killing safe but costs overhead. Waiting risks hanging.
dsh_tool_timeout.Per-tool budgets declared by the tool ve: Per-tool budgets fit what each tool needs but a tool can grant itself too much. A global timeout is predictable but one size fits none.

dsh_tool_pipeline.Walk through what happens between a mode: Admission (policy, approval, guards), dispatch through around-middleware, the tool body, post-execute policies, then one result sent back to the model.
dsh_tool_pipeline.Why must every tool call produce exactly: Otherwise the transcript breaks: the provider rejects it, or the model waits for a result that never comes.
dsh_tool_pipeline.Why do guards run after all pre-execute: A guard is a floor that no middleware can undo. It prevents a plugin from allowing something a security rule forbids.
dsh_tool_pipeline.Which failures go through post-execute a: Denied and cancelled calls go through post-execute, because loop detection needs to see denials. Crashes in the harness itself skip it.
dsh_tool_pipeline.How is an ask decision resolved, and why: Through the approval channel: approved means allow, rejected or cancelled means deny. With no channel it is denied by default, since nobody can approve.
dsh_tool_pipeline.Converting every exception into an error: Error results let the model recover but can hide real bugs. Log crashes loudly even when you return an error result.
dsh_tool_pipeline.Approval per call versus per session ver: Per call is safest and tiring, per session is convenient but abusable, allow-lists are fast but must be maintained.

dsh_repeat_tool_reminder.Why do long-running agents get stuck cal: The model keeps retrying the same thing in a loop. A reminder nudges it to change strategy but still lets a legitimate repeat run.
dsh_repeat_tool_reminder.What counts as the same call here, and w: The same tool with the same arguments. Canonicalizing (sorted keys) makes {a, b} and {b, a} count as the same.
dsh_repeat_tool_reminder.Why must excluded bookkeeping tools neit: Otherwise read, todo, read, todo, read would reset the count each time. The bookkeeping tool would hide a loop.
dsh_repeat_tool_reminder.Why count in post-execute rather than pr: Post-execute sees denied calls as well. Counting before next() makes the reminder reflect this call.
dsh_repeat_tool_reminder.The preview is truncated but the key use: Two calls with different arguments beyond the preview length would look identical and trigger false reminders.
dsh_repeat_tool_reminder.Exact-match detection versus similarity-: Exact match is cheap and precise but misses tiny variations. Similarity catches them but costs more and creates false positives.
dsh_repeat_tool_reminder.The chain lives only in memory and reset: Acceptable for short sessions. Durable tracking needs the chain persisted in the event log and restored on resume.

dsh_open_turn_closers.Why does an agent session log need crash: A crash can leave calls without results. Providers reject a transcript with a tool call that has no result.
dsh_open_turn_closers.Why does the harness distinguish a tool: Never started: safe to say it was not run. Started: it may have side effects, so the model must be told the outcome is unknown.
dsh_open_turn_closers.Walk through which events forget pending: turn/start, turn/end and step/end forget pending calls; a tool/result with surface_op append and the same turn and step answers one. A replace only rewrites an older result, and a result from another step answers a different request.
dsh_open_turn_closers.Why append closers instead of truncating: The log is append-only history. Truncating loses what happened and breaks replay and audit.
dsh_open_turn_closers.How should the model be told to handle a: Say explicitly that it may or may not have run, and to check the state before retrying non-idempotent actions.
dsh_open_turn_closers.Append-only event log with derived conte: A log gives replay, forking and audit, but deriving the context costs work. A mutable list is simple but loses history.
dsh_open_turn_closers.Should recovery happen eagerly on load o: Eager keeps the log valid immediately but does work even if nobody resumes. Lazy delays the work but can surprise readers of the log.

dsh_fold_surface.Why would an agent keep an append-only e: Reproducibility and audit: the log is the truth and the context is a pure function of it, so it can be rebuilt and forked.
dsh_fold_surface.What does 'model-visible means logged' b: Anything the model saw can be reconstructed exactly from the log, so you can debug by replaying.
dsh_fold_surface.Walk through folding append and replace: Append adds nodes; replace swaps a range of nodes currently on the surface. Referencing removed nodes would mean editing text the model never sees.
dsh_fold_surface.Why is a tool-result rewrite allowed to: The call id links the result to its call. Changing it would orphan the pair.
dsh_fold_surface.Why protect the system prompt at node 0: Node 0 anchors the model's instructions and the cached prefix. A range starting there could silently drop the system prompt, so only a system/message replacing exactly that one node is allowed.
dsh_fold_surface.Replaying the full log versus maintainin: Full replay is simple and correct but slow, and incremental folding is fast but risks drift. Snapshots make restarts fast but must stay consistent.
dsh_fold_surface.Replacing ranges in place versus appendi: Replacing in place changes the prefix and invalidates the provider cache. Appending keeps the cache but leaves stale content earlier in the context.

dsh_tool_result_pruner.Why do tool results dominate the context: File reads and command outputs are long. Trimming them first frees context cheaply before a lossy summary.
dsh_tool_result_pruner.Why keep both a head and a tail of the o: The head shows the setup; the tail shows the ending (errors, final results). Keeping only the head drops what usually matters most.
dsh_tool_result_pruner.Walk through how one block's kept head a: Treat the text blocks as one concatenated string, compute the removed range, and map it back per block. Place the marker once, in the first block that overlaps the range.
dsh_tool_result_pruner.Why must head plus marker plus tail fit: Otherwise pruning could make the result longer than the threshold, or never reduce it.
dsh_tool_result_pruner.Why keep the original result in the log: The log stays append-only, so you can still recover the original and replay exactly what the model saw at each point.
dsh_tool_result_pruner.Character budgets versus token budgets f: Characters are fast and deterministic. Tokens match the real cost but depend on the tokenizer and are slower to compute.
dsh_tool_result_pruner.Head-and-tail pruning versus letting the: Head and tail is simple, and paging with offset and limit lets the model read what it needs. Spilling to a file keeps everything available.

dsh_system_prompt_reconcile.What is prompt caching (KV cache prefix: Providers cache the KV of a stable prefix. Changing an early token changes every position after it, so the cache misses.
dsh_system_prompt_reconcile.Why do agent harnesses need to change th: Tools, mode or environment change during a session, for example new skills or a different working directory.
dsh_system_prompt_reconcile.Walk through the four cases: no system n: No node: append; empty rendering: blank every non-empty node; continuing capable route: append only if the effective prompt changed, so the cached prefix survives. Otherwise consolidate: blank later nodes and rewrite the head, one cache miss.
dsh_system_prompt_reconcile.Why blank older system nodes with empty: Blanking keeps node positions and ids stable, so the log and references stay consistent.
dsh_system_prompt_reconcile.Why does a new request series, for examp: The cache is already cold after compaction, so rewriting the head costs nothing extra and gives a clean prompt.
dsh_system_prompt_reconcile.Appending prompt updates versus consolid: Appending is cache-friendly but scatters the instructions. Consolidating is clear but invalidates the cache.
dsh_system_prompt_reconcile.Putting volatile context (time, open fil: Volatile data in the system prompt invalidates the cache on every change. Putting it in later messages keeps the prefix stable, but the model may weight it differently.
